Everyone online is selling you the same thing: a course, a guide, a coaching call. What almost nobody explains is that those are the actual business. This full course walks through the entire model start to finish, including the part most beginners never get shown: how AI removed the single wall that used to stop people before they ever built anything.

You'll learn:
1️⃣ Why digital products quietly outperform dropshipping, trading, and every "hustle" being sold to you right now
2️⃣ The difference between one-time products and recurring-revenue apps, and why the second one changes everything
3️⃣ How to build a real micro-niche app with AI, no code and no developer required
4️⃣ How to turn that app into an actual business with a home base people can find and buy from
5️⃣ Where to host, price, and position your product so the right people show up without paid ads
6️⃣ The exact tools and setup that replaced a $120K, 3-month developer build

Most people think the hard part of this business is the tech. For years, they were right. Building the product meant hiring engineers, waiting months, and spending more than a first product could ever justify. That barrier is gone. The tools now do the building. Your job is the idea, the positioning, and the system that connects it all together.

That's exactly what this course is designed to hand you. If you want to see how the full system connects into one repeatable model, the masterclass linked above breaks down the complete flywheel.

metadata.title: How I Made 10 Million Selling Digital Products (By 22)
metadata.author: Inayah McMillan
metadata.shortDescription:
Learn to start Airbnb for free: https://masterclass.coachinayah.com/class-inayah

Learn to create a clothing brand for free: https://herfirstorder.com/her-first-order-masterclass?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=organic

Shop Inayah: www.inayah.com

No college degree. No investors. Just digital products & a proven system. This is exactly how I went from food stamps and 11 people in one house… to buying a Rolls-Royce, a G-Wagon, and a $500K investment property — all in CASH.

I started by teaching what I knew: Airbnb.
From a simple $27 digital bundle → to a $1,497 course → to backend offers up to $20K, I built a business that made $10M in 3 years.

Selling information is just the beginning. The real wealth comes when you build products that help people implement and succeed.

In this video, I’ll break down:
• The exact funnel that made $3M in 6 months
• Why starting high-ticket is the shortcut to freedom
• The mistake most creators make when scaling
• How I turned info into assets — and created real wealth

Whether you’re a coach, consultant, service provider, or just getting started — this will shift how you see digital products forever.

💬 Drop a comment with your biggest question — I’ll answer it in a future video.

#digitalproducts #airbnbbusiness #entrepreneur #scale  #womeninbusiness #courses

the option to make this page live as a
Notion site. Click the blue publish
button. This turns your page into a
shareable public page.

make sure duplicate as template is

buyers can duplicate your Notion

or payout information, as requested by

everything is accurate so there are no
payout delays later. Once all required
information is entered and your
financial setup is successfully linked,
click save.
Now go back to your product page. In the
top right corner, click the pink publish
and continue button again.
This time, the earlier payment-related
error should be gone and your Notion
template should publish successfully.
At this point, your workflow is

method is connected so you can actually
receive money from sales.

template. If the Notion page opens but

sections, placeholder text, or anything
buyers shouldn't see. Since the page is

intentional and ready for customers.
And that's it. You've now set up your

start to finish. And once people

Selling Notion templates looks like free money — build once, sell forever — but the platform you choose quietly changes what you keep. On Gumroad a $29 template keeps $25.60 from your own link, but only $20.30 when Gumroad's Discover marketplace finds the buyer, because Discover takes a flat 30%. Notion Marketplace takes 8% plus $0.40 and keeps $26.28, but you join a waitlist that can take months.

Pricing follows clear market bands: single-page templates sell for $5-$8, multi-database templates for $10-$18, bundles for $20-$30, and premium systems for $25-$45. The best-selling templates in 2026 target specific niches — freelance invoicing, ADHD daily planning, content creator workflows, real estate CRM — not generic planners. Start 30% below your target price, raise it after your first 10-20 sales and reviews.

The honest timeline: $0-$200 in the first 30 days, $200-$800 by day 90 with consistent posting, and $800-$2,500 a month at 12 months with 10-20 templates live. Where buyers come from matters far more than which checkout you use — Pinterest SEO is the traffic engine most sellers rely on.

Lemon Squeezy—the beloved Merchant of Record platform for digital products, global SaaS taxes, and affiliates—has closed new sign-ups and will stop processing payments on March 31, 2027. not just about collecting money. You

refunds, invoices, compliance, and tax
rules in different countries. This
choice splits our three contenders into
two completely different categories.

processor,
while Paddle and Lemon Squeezy act as a
merchant of record. A merchant of record
means the platform becomes the legal
seller of your product. Instead of you
handling every tax obligation in every

responsibilities on your behalf. If you
choose Stripe Checkout, you get the
lowest transaction fees, usually
starting around 2.9% plus 30 cents. It's
highly customizable,
developer-friendly, and gives you total
control over the customer experience.
This makes Stripe a popular choice for
startups and companies that want
complete flexibility. You can design
your own checkout flow, connect it with
your existing systems, and build a
payment experience that matches your
brand. But there is a massive catch.
Because Stripe only processes the money,
you are entirely responsible for legal
tax compliance. If a customer buys your
software in Europe, Asia, or any US
state, you have to track local tax laws,
register for VAT or sales tax, and file
those tax returns yourself. For a small
business selling in one location, this
may not be a big issue. But once you
start getting customers from multiple
countries, tax compliance can become
complicated very quickly. Different
regions have different rules for digital
products, subscription services,
invoices, and reporting requirements.
Managing all of this manually can take
valuable time away from building your
product. If you don't want that
administrative headache, you look at
Paddle or Lemon Squeezy. Both platforms
act as the official seller of your
product, meaning they take on 100% of
the legal tax liability, calculate,
collect, [music] and pay global taxes
automatically. This can be a major
advantage for solo founders and small
teams that want to sell internationally
without hiring accountants or spending
hours researching tax regulations.
Paddle charges a base fee of 5% plus 50
cents. It's a veteran platform built
with a strong focus on
business-to-business software. It easily
handles custom enterprise contracts,
complex subscription adjustments, and
wire transfers. This makes Paddle a
strong option for SaaS companies selling
to other businesses. If your customers
include larger companies with specific
billing requirements, Paddle provides
tools that support more complex payment
situations. Lemon Squeezy charges the
same base fee of 5% plus 50 cents.
However, it was specifically built for
individual creators and independent
software developers. The user interface
is incredibly modern, and it comes out
of the box with built-in tools for
generating software license keys,
setting up an affiliate network, and
managing simple email marketing
campaigns. This makes Lemon Squeezy
attractive for indie developers
launching apps, plugins, templates, or
digital products. Instead of connecting
multiple services, creators can manage
sales, licensing, and basic marketing
features from one platform.
>> [music]
>> So, which one should you choose? If you
already have a tax account or only sell
locally, Stripe Checkout will save you
money on fees. It is the best choice
when you need maximum customization, and
you are comfortable managing compliance
yourself. But if you sell globally and
want zero tax stress, choose Paddle if
you sell to businesses,
or Lemon Squeezy if you sell to
consumers. Paddle is better suited for
established SaaS companies and B2B
While Lemon Squeezy is a great fit for
independent creators and smaller
software businesses, the right payment
platform depends on your business model,
your customers, and how much control you
want over managing taxes and operations.

make sure to like, subscribe, and share.

Paddle vs FastSpring — which platform handles checkout and taxes better for digital products sold in the US and Canada? We’ll compare fees, ease of use, and compliance features so you can sell with confidence. Watch the full breakdown and subscribe for more digital business insights.


#Paddle #FastSpring #PaddleVsFastSpring #DigitalProducts #Ecommerce #OnlineSales #PaymentProcessing #TaxCompliance #BusinessTools #USCanadaSales

segments.text: If you sell digital products like
software, apps or online courses to
customers in the US and Canada, handling
checkout, payments, and taxes can
quickly become complicated. That is
where platforms like Paddle and
Fastpring come in. Paddle is known as an
all-in-one platform for software and
digital products. It handles payment
processing, checkout, subscriptions, and
tax compliance, so you do not have to
manage multiple tools. When a customer
buys from your store, Paddle
automatically calculates sales tax,
collects the payment, and remits taxes
to the correct authorities in the US,
Canada, and other countries. This makes
selling internationally far less
stressful, especially for small teams
that do not want to worry about
compliance. One of Paddle's biggest
strengths is simplicity. You can create
a checkout page quickly, customize the
look and feel to match your brand, and
start selling without building a
complicated payment flow. It supports
one-time purchases, subscriptions,
trials, and coupon codes, giving you
flexibility for different product
models. Paddle also handles currency
conversion, fraud prevention, and
chargebacks automatically, so you can
focus on growing your business rather
than managing transactions. Paddle gives
detailed analytics as well. You can
track revenue, conversion rates, churn,
and customer behavior all in one
dashboard. This makes it easier to
understand which products are performing
best, optimize pricing, and forecast
growth. For software companies and
digital creators who want a turnkey
solution, Paddle is ideal because it
combines checkout, subscriptions, and
tax handling in a single platform. Now,
let's talk about Fastspring. Fastspring
is another all-in-one e-commerce
platform for digital products, and it
focuses on global sales and flexibility.
Like Paddle, Fastring manages payments,
subscriptions, and tax compliance. It
automatically calculates and remits US
and Canadian sales tax plus VAT and GST
for international sales. This reduces
risk and administrative overhead for
digital sellers.
Fastring stands out for its robust
customization. You can create fully
branded storefronts and checkout
experiences, including upsells, bundles,
and localized pricing. It also supports
a wide range of payment methods, credit
cards, PayPal, Apple Pay, and more, so
customers can pay however they prefer.
Fastring subscription management tools
are strong, offering pration, renewals,
and flexible billing cycles. Another
advantage of Fastspring is its global
support for digital products. If you
plan to expand beyond North America,
Fastpring has expertise in international
compliance, local payment methods, and
multicurrency billing. Its reporting
tools are detailed, giving insights into
revenue, churn, customer location, and
payment methods. Fastspring also
integrates with popular CRM and
marketing tools, helping you automate
workflows from purchase to onboarding.
If your main goal is quick setup,
automatic US and Canadian tax handling,
and easy subscription management, Paddle
is the better choice. If you want
maximum control over your checkout
experience, pricing, and international
expansion, Fastring will give you the
tools you need. Either way, both
platforms make selling digital products
smoother, safer, and more professional
for creators and software companies
alike.

When a customer buys from your store, Paddle automatically calculates sales tax, collects the payment, and remits taxes to the correct authorities in the US, Canada, and other countries. This makes selling internationally far less stressful, especially for small teams that do not want to worry about compliance. One of Paddle's biggest strengths is simplicity. You can create a checkout page quickly, customize the look and feel to match your brand, and start selling without building a complicated payment flow. It supports one-time purchases, subscriptions, trials, and coupon codes, giving you flexibility for different product models. Paddle also handles currency conversion, fraud prevention, and chargebacks automatically, so you can focus on growing your business rather than managing transactions. Paddle gives detailed analytics as well. You can track revenue, conversion rates, churn, and customer behavior all in one dashboard. This makes it easier to understand which products are performing best, optimize pricing, and forecast growth. For software companies and digital creators who want a turnkey solution, Paddle is ideal because it combines checkout, subscriptions, and tax handling in a single platform. Now, let's talk about Fastspring. Fastspring is another all-in-one e-commerce platform for digital products, and it focuses on global sales and flexibility. Like Paddle, Fastring manages payments, subscriptions, and tax compliance. It automatically calculates and remits US and Canadian sales tax plus VAT and GST for international sales. This reduces risk and administrative overhead for digital sellers. Fastring stands out for its robust customization. You can create fully branded storefronts and checkout experiences, including upsells, bundles, and localized pricing. It also supports a wide range of payment methods, credit cards, PayPal, Apple Pay, and more, so customers can pay however they prefer. Fastring subscription management tools are strong, offering pration, renewals, and flexible billing cycles. Another advantage of Fastspring is its global support for digital products. If you plan to expand beyond North America, Fastpring has expertise in international compliance, local payment methods, and multicurrency billing. Its reporting tools are detailed, giving insights into revenue, churn, customer location, and payment methods. Fastspring also integrates with popular CRM and marketing tools, helping you automate workflows from purchase to onboarding. If your main goal is quick setup, automatic US and Canadian tax handling, and easy subscription management, Paddle is the better choice. If you want maximum control over your checkout experience, pricing, and international expansion, Fastring will give you the tools you need. Either way, both platforms make selling digital products smoother, safer, and more professional for creators and software companies alike.

This video breaks down the real differences between the two leading Merchant of Record (MoR) platforms — helping founders, indie makers, and SaaS teams decide which payment solution actually fits their business.

Both platforms handle payments, global taxes, compliance, subscriptions, and invoicing — and even charge the same fee structure (5% + $0.50 per transaction). But once you look deeper, the experience, approval process, payouts, and flexibility are very different.

By the end of this video, you'll know exactly which platform to choose based on your stage, product type, and growth goals.

Built primarily for SaaS businesses

metadata.title: Stripe's Merchant of Record (MoR) Solution: Adding Managed Payments to an Existing App  #mcp
metadata.author: Stephen S.

Stripe's Managed Payments (their new Merchant of Record solution) is in public preview. In this video I wire it into an existing Astro app using the Stripe Power in Kiro.

The Stripe Power reads the pricing tiers already on the marketing site, creates matching products and recurring prices in Stripe via MCP, and generates the checkout endpoint with managed payments enabled. No manual Stripe Dashboard setup for the products.

What I cover:

- Installing the Stripe Power in Kiro and authenticating against a Stripe sandbox
- Using the Power to create products/prices from an existing pricing page
- Setting up a Checkout Session with the managed_payments flag and the right API version
- The tax classification gotcha you'll hit the first time
- What you'd still need for production (user association, webhooks)
- Stripe Managed Payments handles taxes, fraud prevention, and customer transaction support as the merchant of record. You still own the checkout integration and customer relationship.

By the end of this video, you'll know how to:

Build a complete sales funnel from start to finish on Systeme.io.
Set up upsells to increase your average order value.
Add downsells to recover lost sales opportunities.
Implement order bumps to boost conversion rates effortlessly.
If you're looking for more personalized help with your funnel, I can assist you directly. Reach out to me on Fiverr for expert support: https://www.fiverr.com/ground_techy

Don’t forget to like, comment, and subscribe for more tips on sales funnels and automation!

the page we will be redirected to the order form and we won't be able to see the upsell and the second difference is that the upsell does not contain any form so here's a template that I chose for the abso and as you can see here there is no form in this Pages you only find a button to accept the offer and another button to decline the offer and this is why you can't visit the abso directly from the link because your customer must first use the form to fill out their payment information before getting your upsell offer we want this to be as simple as a yes or no decision and having to go through a whole other payment process might not be appealing to someone who's already in purchase mode so for the upsell your customer would just click on the accept offer button and the payment will process immediately but if they decline the offer they will be redirected to our next step in the funnel which is the downsell page the downsell is pretty much the same thing as the upsell page in the sense that the link by itself won't work and there are no for forms in it the different here relies in your sales strategy usually downsells offer a lower price product that might get customers who are on the fence about buying to take action now redirections for both upsell and down sells are made automatically upon decision so when someone accepts the upsell offer they will keep the downsell metadata.title: GoHighLevel One-Click Upsell Setup: Payment Link Redirect + Auto-Delivery Workflow (Part 6)
metadata.author: Social Nest Marketing
metadata.shortDescription:
In Part 6 we set up the first upsell page in the YouTube Ads Launch Kit funnel. I create the upsell product, fix the one-click upsell button (out of the box it skipped straight to the next step), connect it to a payment link that redirects buyers to the second upsell, and build the delivery workflow so buyers get their files automatically.

WHAT YOU'LL LEARN
- Where the upsell page sits in the funnel (right after checkout) and what to customize, including adding your own video
- Why GHL Media Storage doesn't work well for large upsell files (100 MB upload limit, folders can't be sent) and how to use Google Drive links instead
- Creating the $97 upsell product in Payments → Products
- Why the Digital Product delivery option only works with a GHL store (and why I skip it)
- Adding the product to the one-click upsell button
- Fixing the button so it goes to a URL instead of the next funnel step
- Creating a payment link and setting its redirect to the next upsell page
- Running a test purchase to confirm the upsell flow works end to end
- Using ChatGPT + Build Using AI to create the upsell delivery workflow: trigger, tag, custom value and email
- Adding a custom value from the email editor when the workflow won't save it

TIP: The funnel's default preview link works for testing, but connect a custom domain before you go live and update the payment link redirect to match.

This is Part 6 of the YouTube Ads Launch Kit setup series. Part 1 covers the sales page, Part 2 the checkout, Part 3 the order bumps, Part 4 the main product delivery workflow, and Part 5 the AI-built order bump workflows. Next up: the second upsell.

#GoHighLevel #GHL #SalesFunnel

metadata.title: How to Create a One-Click Upsell Funnel for your Shopify store in 2026
metadata.author: LAUNCHTIP
metadata.shortDescription:
Want to build a one-click upsell funnel on your Shopify store that turns single purchases into multi-product orders? In this tutorial, I'll show you how to create a one-click upsell funnel using Sellup — the simple Shopify upsell app that lets you stack offers, accept with a single tap, and skip the friction that kills most upsell flows.

A one-click upsell funnel is the closest thing in ecommerce to a money-printing machine: the customer has already bought, their payment details are on file, and a single tap adds another product to the order. No re-entered card numbers, no second checkout, no second-guessing.

- How to stack multiple offers in sequence for maximum AOV

In this video, I break down my proven strategy for scaling marketing agencies & b2b offers to $1,000,000 per month using self-liquidating funnels. This isn't theory - it's exactly how I've helped multiple businesses add $50K-$100K monthly revenue.

I'll show you the CAC:LTV math that makes or breaks your entire business model. The secret? Spending $2,000 to acquire a customer who immediately pays you $2,000 or more. This creates zero-loss client acquisition where all subsequent revenue becomes pure profit.

Here's what's working for me right now: I spend $6-8K daily on ads, generating qualified calls at $300-350 each. With a 60% show rate and 25-30% close rate, my customer acquisition cost averages $2,000-2,500. But since my initial order value is $2,500, I break even immediately and start profiting from month two.

Cold traffic requires specific offers. I've found one-time setup packages work best because they're low-risk for skeptical prospects. Think "We'll set up your cold email system" or "I'll build your webinar funnel" - simple, specific solutions with clear deliverables.

Remember: your front-end offer isn't your business model - it's just the gateway to acquire buyers at zero cost who you can later upsell to higher-value services.

For marketing channels, I recommend mastering one at a time:

Cold outreach works with minimal budget but requires significant time
Paid ads need at least $200/day but scale efficiently with proven offers
Content marketing builds authority but takes 6+ months to gain traction

Don't believe "free marketing" exists - everything costs either time or money, and scaling means spending capital.

My complete scaling model combines front-end acquisition through qualified ads, optimized fulfillment systems, and revenue expansion through subscriptions and cross-selling. At $1,000/day ad spend, you'll generate around 8-12 new clients monthly. By month two, that's $4-6K monthly recurring revenue with 70% margins.

The profit grows exponentially! To reach $50K monthly profit, you can either continue at the same pace for 17 months or increase ad spend to $5K/day and reach your goal in just 3.4 months.

Avoid these common pitfalls:

Not qualifying prospects (stop wasting money on tire-kickers!)
Trying to do everything simultaneously instead of mastering one channel
Raising prices too quickly and destroying close rates
Misusing guarantees rather than leveraging them strategically
Not creating additional offers to increase customer LTV

This strategy works for every marketing agency, smma, client acquisition business, sales funnel service, or agency owner looking to scale with meta ads and powerful funnels. It's built on simple mathematics - acquire clients at breakeven through self liquidation, retain them with excellent service, and continuously expand revenue through client ascension.

If you're already making $30K/month and want to scale faster, check out my Olympia program at https://JoinOlympia.com where I'll personally help build your offer, funnel, VSL, ads, sales team, and fulfillment systems. This special pricing won't last long, so take action now if you're serious about making money and getting clients at scale.

Want my help to launch your info biz to $200k /y+? Book a Call 👉 https://infoelite.com/start/yt/kmRwEjvxk-w

Watch this video next: https://youtu.be/OogJFTG4nZo

I'm Max Auren. I built an online education business (@theMixElite) from $0 to $1.7M+ that now brings me $30-$50k on autopilot. I made this channel to help other digital info product creators, coaches & course sellers go from $0-$10K to $15–$25K+ per month with clear offers, evergreen funnels, organic content, and automated systems. I won't let you burn yourself to the ground with paid ADs, content hamster-wheel or by spending more time talking with strangers than your loved ones.

Hit me up on Instagram, DMs are open https://instagram.com/maxauren

------------

00:00 funnel results and why paid ads can DOUBLE your biz (fast)
00:34 why paid ads stopped working like they used to
02:27 the self liquidating funnel that builds trust for free
05:18 what to actually sell in your funnel and how to create it
07:27 the simple targeting strategy that actually works

This video breaks down the exact sales funnel that's getting 20,000+ clicks and converting at 14% (over 3,000 sales) with a simple $7 front end offer. The whole setup is designed to build an email list of buyers at break even or better, so you're getting paid to grow your audience instead of bleeding money on ads. I walk through why paid ads got harder over the last 10 years and what actually changed (higher skepticism, more alternatives, lower attention spans), then show you the two deal breakers that kill most funnels before they start.

You'll see my exact landing page structure, from the transformation promise in the ad to the three bonus strategy that gets people to buy. I explain how I turned a YouTube video into a $7 product by making it more in-depth and adding downloads, which means the same content pays me twice (once from ad revenue with 700K+ views, once from the funnel sales). The key is making sure people actually consume what they buy because that's what builds the trust that leads to your main offer sales later.

I cover who to target with Facebook and Instagram ads (spoiler: go broad unless you have zero pixel data), how much to spend per day if you're starting out, and how long to wait before you know if it's working. The math gets interesting when you realize this list is made of people with credit cards who already bought something from you, so even if just 3% end up buying your main course or coaching offer, you're looking at consistent monthly revenue.

At the end I talk about the next step after someone buys your low ticket offer, which is the email sequence that actually drives the high ticket sales. If you're a course creator, coach, or selling digital products and want predictable revenue instead of random sales months, this funnel structure is how you build a list of qualified buyers without losing money on ads.Retry

Have you ever heard of a “perpetual motion machine”?

It’s the holy grail for engineers. 

Basically, this machine is able to keep on working without any additional input of energy. 

Like a Playstation that never needs to be plugged in…

Or a bike that keeps rolling (even uphill) without ever having to be pedalled…

Or a self-liquidating offer (SLO for short)—a marketing funnel tactic designed to pay for itself while still feeding fresh leads into your pipeline and growing your email list….

Pretty cool, right? 

Simply put, an SLO works to immediately monetize traffic coming into your funnel, completely off-setting the cost invested to acquire that traffic.

Put another way, SLO’s are like a bike that pedals itself.  

And they can revolutionize your business. 

Today, I’m going to show you: 

- What a self-liquidating offer (SLO) is and how you can incorporate it into your marketing to bring in zero-cost leads to your funnel that are ready to buy. 

- How these offers tap into multiple principles of marketing that are proven to help businesses scale and thrive. 

- And a few examples of SLOs I’ve come across that do a great job of paying for themselves (while giving the creators the massive marketing power they need to grow).

metadata.title: A Low-Ticket Tiny Offer SLO Funnel Fuels High-Ticket Sales with Allie Bjerk
metadata.author: Mariana Henninger
metadata.shortDescription:
When Allie Bjerk got started, she didn’t wait for the “perfect” offer. She shipped a tiny one — fast. A simple low-ticket product, a clean page, and a clear promise. By breakfast, strangers had bought. By the weekend, she had proof: the idea worked.
In this conversation, Allie breaks down how that one small move reshaped everything — from validating ideas in days, to building a buyer journey that turns low-ticket yeses into sustainable scale. We talk timing, trust, and why you don’t need a massive launch to build real momentum — you need an easy first step that actually helps.

Inside this episode:
 📌 Why a tiny offer is a test — not your final business model.
 📌 Self-liquidating ads 101 — how low-ticket covers acquisition while you learn.
 📌 Turning one “yes” into many — mapping the next step without being pushy.
 
Links mentioned
👉 Grab my Instant YES Machine™️so what you say can take strangers from “meh” to “heck yes!”: https://brandmagnetic.com/yesmachine
👉 Learn more about Allie and her work at: https://alliebjerk.com
👉 Follow Allie on Instagram: https://www.instagram.com/alliebjerk

School focuses on simplicity and community engagement while circle offers a wide range of features and customization options. to get the best info for both of these platforms and see which best aligns with your goals. We'll be providing similarities and differences in the features, the pricing, the pros and the cons. And at the end, you'll be able to choose for yourself. You can check out the links to both services in the description below. And now, let's get started. Now, both school and circle are great for community building and course hosting, but they also differ in various ways. For example, school has a simple user-friendly interface. It has gamification features and calendar for events. Circle on the other hand has more customization options, live streaming and event hosting, membership tiers, direct messaging, analytics and reporting and workflows and automation on higher plans. Talking about plans, here's the detail on the pricing. School has a flat rate of $99 per month for one group, including unlimited members and courses. And a 14-day free trial is available for you to get your feet wet before committing. Circle, on the other hand, has multiple plans. You have the professional at $89 per month with unlimited members and unlimited courses. The business at $199 per month, provides workflows and automations and API access. Enterprise plan comes at $419 per month, and it has advanced analytics, lower transaction fees of 1%. The plus plan comes at a custom pricing. So, you'll need to provide your details for your quote. Now, to our recommendation, if you're prioritizing ease of use and a straightforward approach with unlimited members and courses at a flat rate, school is a solid choice. But for users needing more customization, tiered memberships, and a built-in live streaming, the Circle Professional Plan offers excellent value. And now to the pros and cons. Starting with School. school has a very easy to use interface, simple flat rate pricing, built-in gamification feature which enhances engagement, unlimited members and courses in the base plan, and strong focus on community interaction. On the flip side, it's limited with customization options, no native live streaming, fewer built-in marketing tools. The design can feel basic to some users, and it charges a 2.9% transaction fee on payments. Circle on the other hand on the bright side has a higher customization community spaces offers membership tiers for monetization includes native live streaming and events robust analytics and reporting features and more integrations and automation possibilities although this is available only on the higher tier plans. On the flip side with the cons, it can be more expensive than school especially with transaction fees. interface can be overwhelming for beginners. Also, some advanced features are locked behind higher tier plans and it may require additional tools for comprehensive course building and sales funnels. In conclusion, the best platform really depends on your specific needs and budget. If simplicity and community engagement are your top priorities, school's straightforward approach is appealing. However, if you require more advanced features, customization, and membership options, Circle provides a more comprehensive solution. Now, we have the links to both services in the description below, so you can make your choice after this video. Let us know your thought in the comment section below and thanks for watching.

segments.text: Everyone talks about community, but few
know how to build one that thrives. If
you're building a community on school or
thinking about launching a community,
stop scrolling cuz today I'm going to
share the top seven secrets I used to
turn a ghost town Discord with 25,000
members that are silent into a thriving
paid school community. And how that led
in recurring revenue in just 11 days.
The last secret will make or break your
community. So stay tuned and watch till
the end. Trust me, you won't regret it.
I'm Adnan, School Games winner making
over $45,000 in recurring revenue on
school. And today I'm pulling back the
curtain on exactly how I turned that
chaos into a thriving profitable
community. This isn't theory. This is
battle-tested. And I'm also going to
bring game-changing lessons from Evelyn
Weiss, Max Person, and Charlie Morgan.
Secret number one, kill the noise, build
with intention. My first community
looked good on the outside with 25,000
members on Discord, right? But it was
chaos on the inside. There was no
structure, no transformation, and no
leadership. So I deleted the whole
thing. Then I rebuilt it from scratch on
school with clarity. But this time it
was invite-only access, paid members
only, clear onboarding, simplicity over
chaos. And that shift alone built
instant demand. We had 3,000 people
apply for our waiting list. We crossed
over 1,000 paying members in just 9
days. Secret number two, the 4C
framework that changed everything. This
is inspired by Evelyn Weiss'
transformation systems. I adapted it for
our school community. And it goes like
this. Number one, start with cause. Your
mission must be clear. And for us, it
was to help people build real profitable
POD businesses. Number two, culture. You
need to set expectations. What is
rewarded and what is not tolerated. Make
it so obvious. For us, what's rewarded
was great engagement, publishing wins,
posting motivational posts, and just be
good to one another. What's not
tolerated is self-promotion, spam,
arrogance, and thinking that you know it
all, etc., etc. Number three, you need a
container. For us, it was school because
school simplifies the entire experience.
You've got one login that gives you
everything that you need. Number four,
daily calls, leaderboards, DM check-ins,
member-to-member bonding, and I can go
on and on and on. Now, without these
four C's, you don't really have a
community. You just have a noisy inbox.
Secret number three, onboarding is more
important than content. You can have the
best course in the world, but if people
log in and don't know what to do next,
they literally bounce. And it happened
to us at one point. We were leaking
members fast. Turn was at 17%,
especially when I went to Las Vegas for
the school games, I came back to high
churn cuz I wasn't there in the action.
People were used to seeing me pretty
much every single day, but now they're
not seeing me as much, so they left.
But, we managed to recoup that. We cut
down the churn to 11% by doing this. A
short, clear onboarding video that
explains to them everything from start
to finish, so they will never get lost.
A step-by-step roadmap which shows them
where to go from A to Z. Automated DMs
for inactive members after 48 hours. And
we had the three-day activation path. On
day one, we would send an automated
welcome post with a roadmap and
quick-win activation. For us, that
quick-win activation was we gave our
users one month free of our SaaS. That
really gets them pumped. On day two, we
would do check-in DMs from one of our
customer success staff. And on day
three, we do accountability check-in
from one of our support staff as well.
And as Charlie Morgan says, if you
exceed expectations at every touchpoint,
you win. And that's what we're striving
for. Secret number four, rituals that
drive revenue. Now, this is how we
engineered engagement into our culture.
Number one, we did a niche of the day.
So, for us in the print on demand space,
the entire workflow starts with
research, niche research. So, instead of
them spending about 2 hours a day on
niche research alone, we actually help
them with that. So, we would go and do
the research for them and then just
present it like that for them ready to
chew. In fact, we would chew the food
and just spit it in their mouth for them
to just swallow. Disgusting. This is
actually not my words, it's Alex
Hormozi's words when he was on a live
call giving an example with our
community that this is what we do. We
give our community pretty much
everything ready for them to swallow and
this is how we said it. It was pretty
funny, I thought. So,
another guy that teaches people um how
to do print on demand. And so, he has
like 2% churn in his community. And what
his consumable media was is that every
week or every every I can't remember if
it's every week or every month,
whatever. He would go in and he would
show with his tool how he was finding
the trending uh products or logos or
whatever that were printed and showing
them how to sort for them and then he
would make that into a list and then he
would put it into the community. And so,
the idea there is yet again, how can I
chew the food for them and then spit it
into their mouths?
So, when you give them niches of the day
ready for them to take action, they
really do appreciate it because it helps
them make money fast. We do live Q&As,
community challenges, and giveaways
rewarding good behaviors like
engagements, posting wins, etc. We have
a wins wall. We publicly celebrate every
breakthrough. Whenever someone makes a
sale or makes their first sale, they
post it in the wins wall or the wins
category. You'd be surprised how much
this gets the community pumped. We send
a DM to every member who cancels. We
don't let them disappear without asking
things like, "What happened? How can we
help?" You'd be surprised how many
people you manage to save just by doing
that. And engagement literally isn't
spontaneous, it's structured. You're not
going to wait for people to engage with
your community, you have to engineer it.
So, look for ways inside your community
every single day how you can manufacture
that, how you can create that culture
and instill it within them so that they
can do it without even thinking about it
because it becomes the thing they do.
Secret number five, turn community into
a movement. Max Person talks about
reducing friction. School does that with
tech, but what builds loyalty is
real-life connection. In February, just
last month, I got in my car and drove
from London to Casablanca with no ads,
no promo, and here's what happened. It
was surreal. 120-plus people showed up,
and we had to turn away 100 more. Some
flew from France without any invitation,
just following my Instagram stories to
track the hotel where I was staying at.
It was mind-boggling. That's when I knew
this isn't a group, it's a tribe. Secret
number six, make it about them, not
about you. This is where most creators
go wrong. They build a community around
their content, not their members. Every
post, every video, every email, ask
yourself, what do my members need right
now? How can I make someone feel seen
today? Charlie Morgan says, if every
touch point exceeds expectations, you'll
get rich. And I say, if every touch
point makes someone feel heard, you'll
build something legendary. Secret number
seven, being in the right platform.
That's when leveraging School changed
everything because you have chat,
courses, calendar, leaderboards all in
one place. You've got clean UX, members
actually use it. No more Frankensteining
Discord, Kajabi, Zoom, email tools, and
support threads, etc., etc. The platform
you choose becomes part of your culture,
and School makes it easy to lead,
support, and grow at scale. If this
video helped you, hit that like and
subscribe button. If you want to start
building your own thriving community,
click the link below to try School cuz
when you build it right, they don't just
join, they stay, they thrive, and they
help you grow. Thanks for watching, and
I'll see you in the next one.

metadata.title: Are Free Skool Communities Dying? Why I Turned Mine Paid
metadata.author: Doug Boughton
metadata.shortDescription:
After 7 years of building a free online business Skool community, I'm officially closing that chapter of Fulltime Freedom.

We grew to 6,610 members. But recently, I made one of the biggest decisions in the history of my business.

I removed over 5,400 inactive members and turned my free Skool community into a paid implementation-focused membership.

I want to explain exactly what's changing, why I'm making this decision, what happens next, and the special founding-member opportunity available to you.

ACCESS YOUR FULLTIME FREEDOM COMMUNITY:
https://skool.com/actiontaker

If you're an existing member, click "Upgrade" inside the community to see your membership options.

---

WHAT'S CHANGING INSIDE FULLTIME FREEDOM?

I've spent years teaching people how to build profitable online businesses through webinars, challenges, funnels, and one-to-many selling.

But I've learned something important.

More information isn't what most entrepreneurs need. More IMPLEMENTATION is.

That's why we're moving toward one simple mission:

Helping committed business owners get more qualified traffic, convert that traffic into paying customers, and retain those customers so they can build more predictable revenue and freedom.

Here's what our new membership includes:

✅ Monthly live implementation workshops
✅ Weekly coaching and Q&A sessions with me
✅ A 7-Day Traffic Sprint starting November 23
✅ A 12-week roadmap focused on Traffic → Conversion → Retention
✅ Access to our training vault and past workshops
✅ EventStack AI access for eligible founding members
✅ Opportunities to earn recurring referral commissions
✅ A community focused on action, implementation, and real results

---

YOUR FOUNDING MEMBER INVITATION

As a thank-you for being part of this community, I'm extending special founding-member pricing.

MONTHLY: $47/month
Regular pricing increases to $97/month.

ANNUAL: $284/year
Regular annual pricing increases to $1,000/year.

Both options give you access to the implementation-focused membership described in this video, subject to the founding-member terms.

FOUNDING MEMBER DEADLINE: NOVEMBER 13, 2026

Upgrade inside your community:
https://skool.com/actiontaker/plans

Month-to-month memberships can be canceled anytime.

---

WHAT WE'RE BUILDING TOGETHER

Our focus is simple:

TRAFFIC → CONVERSION → RETENTION

First, we'll help you refine your offer and attract the right people.

Next, we'll build or improve the system that turns those people into paying customers.

Then, we'll focus on keeping those customers, delivering better results, and creating recurring revenue.

No endless collection of courses. No complicated strategy for the sake of complexity.

Just consistent, guided implementation of what matters most.

---

CONNECT WITH ME

Instagram:
https://instagram.com/dougmatthew

Facebook:
https://facebook.com/doug.boughton.5

Business inquiries:
Doug@dougboughton.com

#FulltimeFreedom #SkoolCommunity #OnlineBusiness #BusinessCoaching #Entrepreneurship

🔗 Watch my full Digital Product Masterclass: https://youtu.be/RxypuPGBRPI

Most people building a digital product business in 2026 are running a 2020 playbook... launch a course, stack a guarantee, run ads, repeat. The market moved on. The creators quietly winning right now are doing the opposite of what the gurus taught, and almost nobody is talking about why the old model stopped working. This is everything I've pulled from seven years and well over a thousand hours of studying the businesses that actually scale, from first $500 to $32M+.

You'll learn:
1️⃣ The one foundational step 95% of founders skip before they ever make a sale
2️⃣ Why the simplest funnels quietly out-earn the complicated ones
3️⃣ The platform that's become the printing machine for digital products this year
4️⃣ Why followers stopped mattering, and what the algorithm rewards instead
5️⃣ The shift from promises to proof, and why guarantees now hurt conversions
6️⃣ The AI workflow that takes a product from idea to launch in a single weekend

Most of this comes down to a few counterintuitive shifts: the boring, hyper-specific offer beats the broad one every time. Your profile does more selling than your content. And the real revenue doesn't close on the sales page... it closes in the follow-up most people never do.

The back half of this video gets into the part almost nobody handles correctly: why most creators stall at $5K/month, and the exact order to fix the offer, the backend, and the compounding engine that gets you past it.

If you want to see how the full system connects, especially the AI path for people who don't have their own product yet... that's what the masterclass above walks through, step by step. It's completely free.















Disclaimer: The results mentioned are personal experiences or student case studies. They are not typical and are not guarantees of success. Building a digital product business requires effort, skill, and consistency; individual results will vary.

segments.text: Everyone is telling everyone to sell
digital products, but what no one seems
to be talking about is the reality of
running a digital products business.
I've been selling digital products for
over a decade, and I've been on both
sides of the fence, from making next to
nothing to generating over $20,000 per
month from digital products alone. So,
in this video, I'm going to break down
exactly what goes into running a digital
products business and what that journey
to success actually looks like. But the
first thing that we need to understand
is why digital products in the first
place. There are three main reasons that
I decided to pursue digital products as
a business. The first is passive income.
Now, let me be clear about what I mean
by passive income because there's a lot
of around this term. You've
probably seen people selling this dream
where you press a few buttons and money
just rolls in. But that isn't real. By
definition, passive income is simply
income that isn't directly tied to your
time. You put in the work up front and
it keeps generating money while you're
doing other things. Think of writing a
book or creating a YouTube channel. Same
concept. The second reason is
scalability.
You create something once and you can
sell it to one person or a million
people without any additional work. So
for example, I sell website templates
and when someone purchases one, they get
instant access. They customize it and
launch their website without any input
from me. So if one person buys a
template or a 100 people buy a template,
the amount of work that I do doesn't
change. So there's no limit to how much
I can sell and therefore how much I can
earn. And the third reason is the low
barrier to entry.
Most traditional businesses require
significant upfront investment for
things like inventory, equipment, and
office space, for example. But digital
products, on the other hand, can be
created with minimal, if any, costs.
Again, take my website templates for
example. The only thing it cost me to
create a template is my time. So, for
someone just starting out or with
limited resources, this is perfect. Now,
that all sounds brilliant in theory, but
as I learned the hard way, there's a lot
more to it in practice. My first
experience selling digital products was
11 years ago. Back then, I was a music
producer and I used to create
instrumentals for recording artists. It
had all the same benefits I just
mentioned in terms of passive income,
scalability, and pretty much no cost to
start. But even though it all look good
on paper, the reality was very
different. The single biggest issue I
had was consistency.
And I'm not talking about me being
consistent. I'm talking about making
money consistently. Some months would be
incredible. I'd make four 5 $6,000, but
then the next month I'd barely scrape
together a couple hundred. So, it was
pretty much impossible to rely on this
income because it was so unpredictable.
And as a result, I had to take on client
work just to get by. I tried so many
different things to fix the
inconsistency, like changing my website,
creating content on every social
platform out there, paid ads, and all
sorts, but nothing gave me that
consistency that I was looking for.
Meanwhile, I'm seeing people online
talking about how easy it is to sell
digital products and sharing their 50k
per month screenshots. And I'm there
thinking like there's got to be
something fundamentally wrong with what
I'm doing or I'm missing some sort of
secret that everyone else has figured
out. But what I didn't realize at the
time is that the problem wasn't with my
execution. It was with the type of
problem that I was trying to solve in
the first place. See, in business,
there's a saying that the bigger the
problem you solve, the more money you
make. But what I learned the hard way is
that not all problems are created equal.
There's a massive difference between
solving a nice to-olve problem versus
solving a must-solve problem. So with my
instrumentals, I was solving a nice to
solve problem because most aspiring
artists, they start music as a side
thing. So they don't really need
instrumentals to survive. It's more of a
want than a need. They see music as
their path to success. But until they
make it, they don't have money to invest
into it. So, I was trying to sell a
luxury to people with no money, which
isn't exactly the recipe for consistent
revenue. But when I switched to website
templates, everything changed. All of a
sudden, I was solving a must-solve
problem. For most business owners, their
website is directly connected to how
they make money. It's where their
customers find them, learn more about
them, and decide to buy. So, it's way
more critical to their success. And on
top of that, the audiences are
completely different. Instead of
aspiring artists, I'm dealing with
business owners who already have an
understanding that investing in their
business is how they make more money.
But having a product that solves a
must-solve problem is one thing, but
getting people to see it is another
thing entirely. And this is where it
falls apart for most people. They spend
all their time perfecting their product,
do this huge launch, and then no one
buys. The reality is it doesn't matter
how good your digital product is if
nobody knows it exists. You could create
the most incredible product in the
world, but without an audience, you're
showering into the void. And I'm guilty
of exactly this. Even after I figured
out the right problem to solve with
website templates, I still had to learn
how to get them in front of the right
people consistently. Now, building an
audience can be a whole video in itself.
But there are some key principles that I
learned along the way that really helped
me change the way that I thought about
building an audience. First, I learned
that I needed to build my audience
alongside creating my product, not wait
until after I finished it. And one of
the best ways of doing this is building
in public.

advantages. First, I could get feedback
as I was creating, which means that
people would tell me what they liked,
what they didn't like, and what was
missing before I even finished. And
second, it built hype for the product
before I even launched. Which meant that
by the time that I was ready to sell,
people had already been following the
creation process and were already
interested in buying. And so building in
public turned audience building from
this huge overwhelming cloud into
something that happened naturally while
I worked on my products. The second
thing I learned was to focus on one
platform at a time. I used to try to be
on Instagram, Tik Tok, YouTube, Twitter,
everywhere. But the issue was trying to
keep up with creating content on all
these different platforms was almost
impossible. And what would end up
happening is that I wouldn't really be
building momentum anywhere. But once I
focused on one platform, it made the
whole content creation process feel a
lot more manageable and therefore easier
to stay consistent. And that's when I
started to see real growth. So, we've
spoken about building the right product
and getting it in front of people. But
there's one more thing that's arguably
the biggest killer for people starting a
digital products business, and that is
their expectations.
See, in the online space, you'll see
everyone telling you that you can make x
amount of money in 7 days, 30 days, 90
days, or whatever. And sure, you might
be able to make a few hundred here and
there, but building a real digital
product business that generates
consistent revenue takes time. Real
time. I've been doing this 10 years, and
only within the past few years have I
got to a stage where I'm making
consistent revenue at a high level. But
obviously, that's not to say that it's
going to take you 10 years, because
everyone's journey is different. But the
key is to have realistic expectations
and to understand that this isn't the
get-richqu business model that most
people make it out to be. So think more
along the lines of 6 months, 12 months,
18 months, and that type of timeline.
You have to treat this like a real
business and show up every day. It
requires consistent effort, constant
learning, and the patience to stick with
it. But when you crack it, you wish you
started earlier because honestly,
nothing beats a digital products
business for all the reasons we covered
in this video. If you want to see a
complete behind-the-scenes breakdown of
how exactly I run my website template
business, then check out this video. I
really appreciate your time and I'll see
you there.

metadata.author: Richard Yu
metadata.shortDescription:
🔗 Watch my full Digital Product Masterclass: https://youtu.be/RxypuPGBRPI

📲 Follow me on Instagram: https://www.instagram.com/richardyuzee/

Most people trying to sell digital products in 2026 start with the one question that quietly kills the whole thing before it begins: "What do I want to build?" That instinct feels right... and it's exactly backwards. The operators actually making money flipped the order. They let the market decide first, then built second. This video breaks down the system behind that shift, why Amazon is the wrong place to start, and why "saturated" doesn't mean what most beginners think it means.

You'll learn:
1️⃣ Why the creation-first path is the slowest, most expensive way to start, and what proven operators do instead
2️⃣ How to read a market so it tells you exactly what to build before you write a single page
3️⃣ The difference between copying a product and modeling demand (and why one is how every great company was built)
4️⃣ The three levers... angle, packaging, positioning... that turn a crowded niche into your own category
5️⃣ How AI collapses weeks of product creation into a single afternoon
6️⃣ The free validation pass that saves you months of building something nobody wants

The reason most people stay stuck isn't the market... it's that they're solving a problem nobody is searching for at 11pm on a Tuesday. There's a real difference between "how to get fit" and the specific, urgent pain a buyer will actually pay to solve, and once you see it, you can't unsee it. The same logic runs through everything here: the niche, the product, the traffic, the validation. None of it requires a degree, a big audience, or showing your face.

What makes this work now is that the barrier to entry has never been lower... but lower barrier means the people who understand the system win, not the people chasing the trend. That's the part that doesn't fit inside one video.

If you want to see how the full system connects end-to-end, including real student case studies and the complete traffic model, that's exactly what the masterclass above walks through.
















Disclaimer: The results mentioned are personal experiences or student case studies. They are not typical and are not guarantees of success. Building a digital product business requires effort, skill, and consistency; individual results will vary.

If you’ve tried before but struggled, you’re not alone. This guide is step-by-step, tested, and practical. We’ll choose a money niche, create products, list them, market them, and scale. Profitable niches exist where hungry buyers meet recurring needs. Think simple, useful, repeat-purchase niches. Planners, resume kits, AI prompts, and meal plans. Your products should deliver outcomes: eBooks, templates, planners, or short courses. In just forty-eight hours, you can go from idea to your first published product. Done is better than perfect. Go where buyers already are: Gumroad, Etsy, Shopify. Platforms made for creators. Optimize your listing: lead with benefits, show strong visuals, use SEO tags, and always add a clear call to action. Here’s how fast it is to set up. Title, upload, price, publish. Done. Marketing is simple. Use short-form content on TikTok and Instagram, capture emails, and funnel them to your offers. Every viral post follows the same formula: problem, promise, proof. Post daily—demos, tips, stories, objections handled, behind-the-scenes, and clear CTAs. Email funnels are simple: freebie, welcome, nurture, then offer. Build trust, then make the sale. Once you’re ready, scale with ads, partnerships, bundles, and upsells. A small tweak in your product title can double clicks. Simple shifts make a big difference. One student launched a planner template and made their first ten sales within days. Now you have the complete roadmap from zero to ten thousand dollars. Grab the one-hundred-page blueprint packed with strategies, examples, and action steps. Start today. The link is in the description. And if you’re ready for your next step, watch this: how to pick a money niche in fifteen minutes.

metadata.title: Lemon Squeezy is closing. Can you just run your own checkout?
metadata.author: heyymilian
metadata.shortDescription:
Lemon Squeezy stops processing transactions on 31 March 2027, and its own page says there will be no extensions. The founder answer is: build my own checkout. You can. But a checkout is the form that takes the money; a merchant of record is who carries the tax, the fraud and the disputes behind it, and you can't self-host that part.

This video goes through what a merchant of record does (in Stripe's own words), the key dates, what Stripe Managed Payments doesn't cover, what you take back if you build on Stripe Checkout and Stripe Tax, the fees as the pages print them, and what I would do by situation.

Chapters
0:00 Lemon Squeezy is closing
0:32 What a merchant of record does
1:27 The dates
2:18 The like-for-like gap
3:13 Build it yourself
4:18 Fees, side by side
5:31 What I would do

Sources (all captured 23 Nov 2026; check them again before you decide, they change)
- Lemon Squeezy migration guide: https://docs.lemonsqueezy.com/migration (processing stops 31 Mar 2027, no extensions; 16 Nov 2026 no new sign-ups; 2 Dec 2026 migration tooling; mid-January 2027 recommended latest start; up to 8 weeks; PayPal, storefronts, digital fulfillment and affiliates not in Managed Payments; 1.5% promotional price for migrating merchants through 1 Dec 2027 plus standard processing fees)
- Lemon Squeezy goodbye post (JR Farr, 16 Nov 2026): https://www.lemonsqueezy.com/blog/saying-goodbye-to-lemon-squeezy
- Lemon Squeezy pricing: https://www.lemonsqueezy.com/pricing (5% + 50 cents per transaction, list price)
- Stripe Managed Payments: https://stripe.com/managed-payments (merchant of record wording, Stripe Tax vs Managed Payments)
- Managed Payments eligibility: https://docs.stripe.com/payments/managed-payments/eligibility
- Stripe pricing: https://stripe.com/pricing (2.9% + 30 cents per successful transaction for domestic cards, +1.5% international, +1% currency conversion; Managed Payments 3.5% in addition to Payments fees; 15.00 USD per dispute received; list prices as printed on the page)
- Stripe Tax pricing: https://stripe.com/tax/pricing (Tax Basic 0.5% no-code or 50 cents API per transaction where you're registered; Tax Complete starting at 90 USD per month)
- Stripe Tax: https://stripe.com/tax

Our own arithmetic, labelled "calculated" in the video, one domestic card payment, no volume assumed: 3.5% + 2.9% + 30 cents = 6.4% + 30 cents; 2.9% + 30 cents + 0.5% = 3.4% + 30 cents; 23 Nov 2026 to 31 Mar 2027 = 128 days. Build hours for a self-built checkout: not tracked, so no number.

This is not legal or tax advice. It says what each option takes on and points at the pages.

The voice in this video is AI-generated (ElevenLabs), from a script we wrote. Graphics made with HyperFrames.

Lemon Squeezy stops processing payments on March 31, 2027, and Stripe Managed Payments, the official replacement, has no license keys, no affiliates and no PayPal subscriptions. I go through the dates, what the Stripe path costs on a $99 sale, and where I'd move depending on what you sell: Dodo Payments, Creem, Polar, Paddle, Freemius or your own WordPress checkout.

FluentCart (affiliate link): https://gauravtiwari.org/go/fluentcart/
Core Forms (my own plugin): https://gauravtiwari.org/go/core-forms/

Some links are affiliate links. Core Forms is my own plugin.

Fees are each provider's published rates in November 2026, on a US card. This is general information and it isn't tax advice.

00:20 Key Dates

00:59 What Doesn't Move

01:39 What Stripe Costs

segments.text: Lemon Squeezy is shutting down. It closed new sign-ups on November 16th,
and on March 31st, 2027, it stops processing every payment,
subscription renewals included. Lemon Squeezy says that date won't move.
So if your store runs on it, you have about four months, and the migration alone
takes four to eight weeks
Three dates matter. On December second, the migration tooling for Stripe Managed
Payments opens. Mid-January is the latest start Lemon Squeezy recommends,
and March thirty-first is the last day.
I'd treat mid-January as the real deadline because a February start leaves no time to
fix a failed import
The official replacement is Stripe Managed Payments.
Stripe bought Lemon Squeezy in 2024, and here Stripe becomes the merchant of
record, so it handles the sales tax work for you.
Lemon Squeezy's tooling moves your products, your customers, and your card
subscriptions, and customers get at least 14 days notice.
The harder part is what doesn't come along.
Managed Payments has no license keys and no file delivery.
It has no affiliates. PayPal subscriptions can't move, so those subscribers have to
buy again, and nothing redirects. Every checkout link, button, and webhook
has to be replaced by hand
It also depends on where your business is registered.
Stripe's list covers the United States, Canada, the UK, most of Europe,
Australia, Hong Kong, Japan, and Singapore.
India isn't on it, and neither are Brazil or the United Arab Emirates.
I sell my plugins from India, so this path isn't open to me.
It's also for digital products only
Now the fees. On a $99 sale, Lemon Squeezy takes
$5.45 today. Stripe takes $4.66 on the migration rate,
and that rate ends on December 1st, 2027.
After that, it's $6.64. So Stripe is cheaper for about a year and
about 20% more expensive after it
Before you compare providers, I'd settle one question.
Do you rent a merchant of record again, or do you own your checkout?
A merchant of record is the legal seller.
It files your taxes and fights your chargebacks, and it takes 4 to 6% of every
sale. Your own checkout costs about 3%, and the tax work becomes yours
If you rent again, here's how I'd choose.
When customers already hold license keys, I'd look at Dodo Payments first.
Its migration tool imports your active Lemon Squeezy keys along with products,
customers, and coupons. It charges 4% plus 40 cents, it takes PayPal,
and it accepts businesses in India. One catch: imported keys lose their
activations, and the tool is still in beta
For the lowest flat fee, it's Creem: 3.9% plus 40 cents,
with nothing extra for international cards.
But it has no PayPal, and active subscriptions don't move.
Polar is built for developers. Its free plan matches Lemon Squeezy's rate, and the
$20 plan drops to 3.8% plus 40 cents
Paddle is the most established name here at the same 5% plus 50 cents.
It has PayPal, but no license keys. And for WordPress plugins and themes,
there's Freemius. It handles licensing and updates, and on a $99 plugin,
it keeps about $10. I haven't sold through Freemius myself
Or you own the checkout. If you already run WordPress, your site can take the
payment and issue the keys. On that same $99 sale, Stripe keeps about
$3.17. I sell my own plugins this way through FluentCart.
Easy Digital Downloads is the long-standing choice, and Core Forms,
which is my own plugin, does checkout and licensing too.
None of them imports from Lemon Squeezy, so the move is manual
Whichever way you go, the order matters more than the tool.
Export everything now: customers, orders, subscriptions, and license keys.
Turn PayPal off at checkout so new subscribers can migrate.
Set up the new provider in test mode. Replace every link.
Then email your customers and tell them the new name on their card statement
If you're still unsure, I'd let your license keys decide and let the fee come
second. And keep three things in your own hands from now on: your customer list,
your license server, and your checkout links.
The full comparison with every fee and a free migration checklist is linked in the
description

Stripe takes $4.66 on the migration rate, and that rate ends on December 1st, 2027. After that, it's $6.64. So Stripe is cheaper for about a year and about 20% more expensive after it Before you compare providers, I'd settle one question. Do you rent a merchant of record again, or do you own your checkout? A merchant of record is the legal seller. It files your taxes and fights your chargebacks, and it takes 4 to 6% of every sale. Your own checkout costs about 3%, and the tax work becomes yours If you rent again, here's how I'd choose. When customers already hold license keys, I'd look at Dodo Payments first. Its migration tool imports your active Lemon Squeezy keys along with products, customers, and coupons. It charges 4% plus 40 cents, it takes PayPal, and it accepts businesses in India. One catch: imported keys lose their activations, and the tool is still in beta For the lowest flat fee, it's Creem: 3.9% plus 40 cents, with nothing extra for international cards. But it has no PayPal, and active subscriptions don't move. Polar is built for developers. Its free plan matches Lemon Squeezy's rate, and the $20 plan drops to 3.8% plus 40 cents Paddle is the most established name here at the same 5% plus 50 cents. It has PayPal, but no license keys. And for WordPress plugins and themes, there's Freemius. It handles licensing and updates, and on a $99 plugin, it keeps about $10. I haven't sold through Freemius myself Or you own the checkout. If you already run WordPress, your site can take the payment and issue the keys. On that same $99 sale, Stripe keeps about $3.17. I sell my own plugins this way through FluentCart. Easy Digital Downloads is the long-standing choice, and Core Forms, which is my own plugin, does checkout and licensing too. None of them imports from Lemon Squeezy, so the move is manual Whichever way you go, the order matters more than the tool. Export everything now: customers, orders, subscriptions, and license keys. Turn PayPal off at checkout so new subscribers can migrate. Set up the new provider in test mode. Replace every link. Then email your customers and tell them the new name on their card statement If you're still unsure, I'd let your license keys decide and let the fee come second. And keep three things in your own hands from now on: your customer list, your license server, and your checkout links. The full comparison with every fee and a free migration checklist is linked in the description

Lemon Squeezy vs Payhip in 2026: what do you actually keep from a $20 sale? Math from public pages only. Lemon Squeezy charges 5% + 50 cents per transaction with no monthly fee, so you keep $18.50. CHAPTERS

4:48 What the 50 cents buys

6:11 One more thing to check

SOURCES (all checked Nov 14, 2026; prices change, so check the date)

OUR MATH (US seller, buyer and card; one-time $20 digital product; no tax added; Payhip on Stripe, cheapest plan per volume; no refunds, PayPal, international cards or payout fees)
Per $20 sale: Lemon Squeezy 5% + $0.50 = $1.50, you keep $18.50. Payhip Free: 5% = $1.00 + Stripe 2.9% + $0.30 = $0.88, you keep $18.12; Plus (2%, $29/mo) $18.72; Pro (0%, $99/mo) $19.12 (before each plan).
Per sale at other prices (Lemon Squeezy / Payhip Free / Plus / Pro keep): $10: $9.00 / $8.91 / $9.21 / $9.41; $20: $18.50 / $18.12 / $18.72 / $19.12; $50: $47.00 / $45.75 / $47.25 / $48.25; $100: $94.50 / $91.80 / $94.80 / $96.80

segments.text: Here's a $20 digital product, sold on Lemon Squeezy and on Payhip. Same buyer, same U.S. card.
Lemon Squeezy takes one flat fee, 5% plus 50 cents. That's $1.50,
so you keep $18.50, with no monthly plan.
Payhip's free plan takes 5%, a dollar, and Stripe takes 88 cents more.
You keep $18.12. So on the free plan, Lemon Squeezy wins this one, by 38 cents. Our math.
This is educational, not financial, legal or tax advice.
We hold no position in Lemon Squeezy or Payhip,
and the narration is an AI voice.
Disclosure: the Payhip link in the description is an affiliate link,
so the channel may earn a commission if you sign up.
The Lemon Squeezy link isn't an affiliate link. Neither changes these numbers.
Every number comes from Lemon Squeezy's, Payhip's and Stripe's own pages,
checked November 14, 2026.
Derived totals are labeled our math. Prices change,
so treat the check date as part of the source.
Start with Lemon Squeezy's pricing page.
Ecommerce is 5% plus 50 cents per transaction.
There are no monthly charges. It only takes a cut when you sell.
The help center says that fee is calculated on the total order value.
If the buyer pays tax, the 5% applies to that too.
It also lists extras: 1.5% more for international cards, 1.5% more for PayPal,
and 0.5% more for subscriptions.
Payouts are separate. Through Stripe, they're free to a U.S. bank account.
Through PayPal, there's a flat 50 cents per payout for U.S. accounts.
And one more catch for cheap products.
The help center says that if you sell products lower than $10,
you should contact sales for custom pricing.
So check what you'd actually be quoted before you launch.
Now Payhip. Free Forever is zero dollars a month, plus a 5% transaction fee.
Plus is $29 a month, and cuts the fee to 2%.
Pro is $99 a month, with no transaction fee.
Payhip says there's no feature-gating. You get all of its features,
even on the free plan, so the plan only changes the fee.
But PayPal and Stripe still charge their standard rates, on all plans.
Stripe's U.S. rate is 2.9% plus 30 cents per domestic card. On $20,
that's 88 cents. Our math.
So line up one $20 sale. Lemon Squeezy keeps you $18.50, with no monthly plan.
Payhip Free keeps $18.12.
Plus keeps $18.72, before its $29 a month.
And Pro keeps $19.12, before its $99 a month.
That's 62 cents more per sale than Lemon Squeezy,
but only once you've covered the plan. Our math.
The flat 50 cents matters most on cheap products.
Here's the same math at four prices. Our math.
At $10, Lemon Squeezy keeps $9. Payhip Free keeps $8.91.
At $100, Lemon Squeezy keeps $94.50. Payhip Free keeps $91.80,
but Pro keeps $96.80.
Now the real monthly bill, with $20 products, U.S. cards,
and Payhip's cheapest plan at each level. Our math.
At $200 a month, ten sales, Lemon Squeezy costs $15. Payhip Free costs $18.80.
Lemon Squeezy is $3.80 ahead.
At $1,000, Payhip's best is Plus, at $93. Lemon Squeezy is $75.
Lemon Squeezy by $18.
At $2,000, Plus costs $157 against $150. Lemon Squeezy by $7.
At $2,640, 132 sales, Lemon Squeezy costs $198. Payhip Plus costs $197.96.
That's where Payhip first gets cheaper.
At $5,000, Payhip Pro costs $319 in all, against $375. Payhip by $56.
And at $10,000, Pro costs $539 against $750. Payhip by $211.
That tipping point moves with price. Our math.
With $10 products, Payhip pulls ahead at 139 sales a month.
At $20, it's 132 sales.
At $50, it's just 80 sales.
And at $100, 44 sales. Below those, Lemon Squeezy costs less.
So what does Lemon Squeezy's higher flat fee buy?
It's the merchant of record for every sale.
Its help center says you don't have to worry about collecting and remitting
sales tax, including international tax like VAT. Lemon Squeezy takes care of it.
Payhip's tax page is narrower, but real. It handles digital EU and UK VAT,
and assumes full responsibility for collecting, reporting and paying it.
In the U.S., it says it's a marketplace facilitator. In Canada,
a digital platform operator.
Chargebacks are the other big difference.
Lemon Squeezy says it's generally responsible for handling them.
But in most cases it deducts the refunded amount, minus its platform fee,
plus a $15 dispute fee from your next payout.
It also reserves the right to issue refunds itself within 60 days of purchase,
at its own discretion, to prevent chargebacks.
And it warns that even with a no-refunds policy,
customers can issue chargebacks at any time.
And if your store has too many chargebacks,
Lemon Squeezy says it may suspend your account.
On Payhip, payments run through your own processor.
Its help center says it does not directly manage or process payments.
Stripe's own fee is $15.00 for each dispute you receive.
So the fee is the same $15. The difference is who handles the dispute.
One more thing. In a January 28, 2026 post,
Lemon Squeezy's CEO wrote that the company is building Stripe Managed Payments with Stripe.
He calls it Stripe's merchant of record solution.
Lemon Squeezy's pricing page still shows 5% plus 50 cents today,
so check it live before you pick.
Here's what these numbers leave out.
If the buyer pays tax, Lemon Squeezy's 5% applies to the total, tax included.
International cards add 1.5%, on Lemon Squeezy and on Stripe.
PayPal sales add 1.5% on Lemon Squeezy.
Subscriptions add 0.5% on Lemon Squeezy.
And payout fees, refunds and income taxes aren't in here either.
So which one?
Lemon Squeezy fits if you want tax and chargebacks handled for you.
If you sell at lower volume, under the tipping point.
And if you never want a monthly plan.
Payhip fits if your volume is past the tipping point.
If you want to cap your fees with a flat $99 plan.
And if you're fine using your own Stripe or PayPal account.
So neither wins everywhere. On a $20 product,
Lemon Squeezy costs less until about $2,640 a month, and Payhip costs less after.
It depends on your price, your volume, and who you want handling the risk.
Every page I showed is linked in the description, with the date I checked it.
Prices change, so check before you pick.
If you're also weighing Gumroad,
the Payhip versus Gumroad breakdown is on the channel.
Thanks for watching.
